questions.question: I’ve been weighing how to scale up sustainable hydrogen generation beyond traditional fossil fuel cracking, especially when looking at biological routes that can simultaneously clean industrial runoff. The catalytic dehydrogenation of aviation fuels is promising for clean fuel cell feedstocks, but it still relies on complex hydrocarbon processing and expensive catalyst designs. Meanwhile, the broader agricultural sector is struggling to decarbonize fertilizer manufacturing by swapping out conventional hydrogen pathways for low-carbon alternatives across multiple production tiers. This brings me back to the biological electrochemical approach, where microbial communities on specific electrode surfaces drive the split of organic waste streams into usable gas. Given the trade-offs between nanomaterial coatings and standard carbon substrates, which anode configuration actually maximizes current output and gas yield when treating actual fermentation byproducts rather than idealized lab solutions?
